title: Glucose-responsive probiotics for glycaemic modulation in mice and monkeys.
data_url: https://static-content.springer.com/esm/art%3A10.1038%2Fs41586-026-10909-6/MediaObjects/41586_2026_10909_MOESM1_ESM.pdf (plus MOESM3, MOESM5-MOESM12 source-data files at the same path pattern)

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Downloaded and opened all 10 freely accessible supplementary files (1 Supplementary Information PDF, 36 pages; 1 statistics workbook; 7 source-data workbooks; 1 ZIP holding 5 more workbooks). Counted every sheet and every numeric cell with openpyxl: 81 sheets, 3,836 numeric values in total, each sheet being one figure panel (e.g. sheet '2d' = blood glucose over time for 5 mice given buffer vs 5 given the engineered bacteria). Extracted the PDF text and listed all 18 supplementary tables; they are blood counts, serum chemistry, blood glucose time courses, a 23-row plasmid list and a qPCR primer list. Queried NCBI elink from the PubMed record (ID 42587154) to GEO, SRA, BioProject and BioSample: zero links. Searched Zenodo (by DOI and by keyword) and Dryad: zero hits. Figshare's search endpoint returned HTTP 404.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: The abstract only (Europe PMC flags the paper as not open access, not in PMC, no full text). The Nature article page redirects to a login, so I never saw the Data Availability statement, the Methods, or the exact animal numbers stated in the main text. Everything about the data volume below comes from the files I opened, not from the paper.

a1_downloadable.note: PASS, verified: all 10 supplementary/source-data files download from Springer's static content server with no login (HTTP 200, 3.9 MB PDF plus ~0.4 MB of spreadsheets). The article text itself is paywalled, but the data files are not.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: FAIL, verified in the files. There is no prediction target anywhere as a column. Each of the 81 sheets is a figure panel with merged, unlabelled headers (a time column, then repeated unnamed columns that are individual mice or wells, grouped under a treatment name sitting one row above). Any label would have to be hand-built by reading each panel's layout and re-keying it. There is no identifier linking a row in one sheet to a row in another.

a3_inputs_present.note: FAIL, verified. The only candidate modelling input would be the design of the engineered genetic parts, but Supplementary Table 17 gives them as text descriptions ('PhexR4(Ptac-4xHexO)-RBS-sfGFP'), not as DNA sequences. No promoter, operator or ribosome-binding-site sequences are deposited anywhere I could find. For the animal data, the only 'input' is a treatment group name and a timepoint.

a4_units_stated.note: PASS, verified but weakly. Most sheets label a unit in a header cell ('Time (h)', 'Glucose (mM)', 'x10^4' as a scale factor), though the measured quantity itself is usually unnamed and must be inferred from the figure caption in the (paywalled) main text.

a5_enough_rows.note: FAIL, verified by counting. 3,836 numeric values total, but that is every individual measurement across 81 unrelated figure panels, not rows of a feature/label table. The real unit of analysis is an animal or a culture well: group sizes are 3-10 (e.g. 5 diabetic and 5 non-diabetic monkeys in sheet '5h'; 3 replicates per glucose concentration in sheet '1c'). The checklist needs ~1,500 labelled rows; this is two to three orders of magnitude short.

a6_fits_laptop.working_set: ~4.3 MB of spreadsheets plus a 3.9 MB PDF
a6_fits_laptop.note: PASS, verified. Trivially small. This is the only thing the dataset has going for it.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: Cannot be properly checked: the main text is paywalled so there is no stated count to compare against. The supplementary statistics workbook (MOESM3) lists the test and group comparison for every panel and is internally consistent with the source-data sheets I opened.

a8_label_provenance.note: PASS in principle, verified. Every value is a direct physical measurement (blood glucose by glucometer, luminescence/fluorescence from reporter genes, enzyme-linked immunoassay for GLP-1, colony counts). Nothing is another model's output. This killer is not the problem here.

existing_models.name: Deep-learning models for synthetic bacterial promoter strength (e.g. the 2025 Nucleic Acids Research work on programmable design of Escherichia coli core promoters, and the 2021 ACS Synthetic Biology de novo synthetic promoter library plus machine learning)
existing_models.score_and_split: Reported Pearson correlations around 0.84-0.94 according to the search-result summaries; I did not retrieve the full papers, so I have not verified the numbers or the splits they used.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Not verified — I did not read the discussions.

integration.partner_dataset: None usable — there is no standard identifier (no UniProt accession, no gene ID, no sequence) anywhere in the deposited files to join on.
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Cannot be written; the deposited data carries no identifier that links it to any external resource.

controls.positive_control: The data does contain a known effect a model should recover — reporter output rises monotonically with glucose concentration, and diabetic (db/db) mice show higher blood glucose than wild-type — but with 3-10 values per group there is nothing to train on.
controls.negative_control: Label shuffling would be meaningless at this sample size.
controls.external_validation: None: no second dataset, no repository deposit, no publication-year or source column.

honest_claim_h3: No honest modelling claim can be made from these files: the deposited data are 81 separate figure panels of 3-10 animals or wells each, with no features, no shared key and no prediction target.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use engineered bacterial genetic-circuit design to predict how strongly the circuit switches on when blood sugar rises.
plain_idea.train_on: The project I considered would train on the design of each engineered genetic part (how many copies of the HexR regulator's DNA binding site sit in the promoter, which ribosome binding site was used) paired with its measured reporter output. Verified count of such designs: 23 plasmids, of which about 9 vary the promoter or ribosome binding site.
plain_idea.predict: Predicted output would be the fold-change in reporter signal (fluorescent protein or luminescence) between low and high glucose, measured by plate reader in bacterial culture — a real physical measurement, reported in the source-data sheets.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Synthetic-biology groups building 'sense-and-respond' living drugs currently tune these circuits by building and testing one variant at a time; a predictor would shortcut that. But this paper supplies roughly nine designs, which is a scatter plot, not a training set.

ml_idea: Considered and rejected: predict glucose-induced fold-change of an engineered bacterial sensor circuit from its promoter architecture (number of HexR operator repeats) and ribosome binding site. Dead on arrival because the paper reports about 9 such design variants with 3 replicates each, and gives their DNA sequences only as shorthand descriptions, not as sequence.

effort.compute_note: Measured, not estimated: the whole supplement is 4.3 MB and opened in seconds with openpyxl. The 12 hours is a guess at hand-transcribing 81 merged-header figure panels into tidy tables, which would still leave too few rows to model.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Count the numeric cells per sheet and the group sizes. Done: 3,836 values over 81 figure panels, groups of 3-10 animals or wells. That is the whole evaluation.

verdict_reason: Fails Part A on three killers, all confirmed by opening the files rather than reading the paper. A2: there is no prediction target as a column — the deposited data are 81 per-figure panels with merged, unlabelled headers and no key joining them. A3: the one plausible modelling input, the engineered promoter and ribosome-binding-site designs, appears only as text shorthand ('Ptac-4xHexO'), never as DNA sequence. A5 is the decisive one: 3,836 numeric values in total, but the unit of analysis is an animal or a culture well, with 3-10 per group — roughly nine distinct circuit designs and a few dozen monkeys and mice. This is an excellent in-vivo therapeutics paper and a poor machine-learning substrate; no sequencing or omics data was deposited to NCBI, Zenodo or Dryad to rescue it.
